title: Modeling CO Line Luminosity with FIRE simulations: II. Comparison With Observations, CO Luminosity Functions and Redshift Evolution
abstract: We present predictions for the CO(1-0) and CO(2-1) luminosities of 765, 850, 887 and 915 galaxies at z=0, 1, 2 and 3, respectively, drawn from the Feedback in Realistic Environments (FIRE-2) simulations and post-processed with SKIRT radiative transfer and CLOUDY line emission calculations. We compare our CO line luminosity predictions with existing observations. At z=0, our predictions reproduce the observed scatter and mean relation between star formation rate (SFR) and CO(1-0) luminosity for both massive star-forming galaxies and low-metallicity dwarf galaxies. We also reproduce the observed superlinear power-law slope between CO(1-0) luminosity and metallicity. At z=1, our CO(2-1) predictions scatter to much lower luminosities than observed, which likely reflects the limited sensitivity of current surveys. At fixed SFR, our CO(1-0) luminosities decrease by roughly an order of magnitude per unit increase in redshift. This decline is likely driven by the decrease in metallicity with increasing redshift, since FIRE-2 galaxies with comparable SFR and metallicity produce similar CO(1-0) luminosities regardless of redshift. At fixed stellar mass, the predicted luminosities show no redshift dependence. These results show that our FIRE-2 predictions reproduce the observed scaling relations between CO(1-0) luminosity and galaxy properties wherever the observed galaxies are robustly detected. This gives us confidence in our predictions for the regime where no observational data exist, and suggests that our luminosity predictions can be used to build predictive models for CO line intensity mapping experiments.

title: The L1157 filament as traced in HNCO by the LMT
abstract: Context. The L1157 outflow is a prototype of chemically active outflows where to look for molecular species linked to complex chemistry. Aims. With the aim of imaging the large (parsec) scale structure of key prebiotic molecules, we have mapped the whole blue-lobe of the L1157 outflow with the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT), proving the potential of this facility to detect weak and extended molecular emission. Methods. Isocyanic acid, HNCO, an important precursor of complex chemistry, was chosen to be observed in its (4_0,4-3_0-3) transition at 87.925 GHz with the SEQUOIA focal-plane array, covering an area of 3x3 arcmin2 centered at the position of the main shock L1157-B1, which included a large portion of the vicinity of the protostellar region. Results. The HNCO emission was detected not only from the outflow but it also was found tracing a structure of about 0.3 pc in length, corresponding to the filament from which the protostellar system was born. Conclusions. The HNCO molecule was found to be a tracer of the densest part of filaments in molecular clouds, and given its importance in the formation of more complex molecules, its presence in the cold, quiescent filamentary gas indicates that the building blocks of complex chemistry are already well established in stages prior to protostellar warming or shocks. By allowing the detection of structures related with the filament, these observations proved the LMT potentialities to map weak and extended components in molecular clouds.

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Mass-to-light ratio of elliptical galaxies: constraints from strong lensing
abstract: Mass is among the most fundamental properties describing a galaxy. The relation between the luminosity and the total mass of a galaxy contains information on the efficiency of the star formation process and on the distribution of dark matter. We used strong gravitational lensing data from the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) to constrain the total mass enclosed within an aperture of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc, $M_5$, of elliptical galaxies. Our analysis is based on a sample of 95 lenses, which we built by ensuring that their selection function is reproducible. This enabled us to correct our inference for selection effects. The average $\log_{10}{(M_5\,h\,M_\odot^{-1})}$ for a galaxy with an $r$-band luminosity of $10^{10.7}L_{\odot}\,h^{-2}$ at $z=0.5$ is $11.30\pm0.02$. The mass $M_5$ scales with luminosity to the power $β_\mathrm{L}=0.71\pm0.07$, and decreases with increasing redshift at fixed luminosity. Assuming a scenario in which galaxies grow by mergers and stellar populations evolve passively, these correlations imply that $M_5$ increases with time for individual galaxies. These measurements provide a useful benchmark for testing models of galaxy structure and evolution that make predictions on the distribution of total mass on the scales of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc.

title: A VLT/CRIRES+ study of helium 1.083$μ$m absorption features towards the inner Orion Nebula
abstract: JWST NIRCam F115W observations towards the inner Orion Nebula revealed a diverse array of previously unknown dark features. The most likely cause was absorption or suppressed emission of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet which lies in that filter. We have obtained VLT/CRIRES+ high-resolution spectrographic observations over a selection of different dark targets, confirming that the features are indeed explained by a reduction in the flux of the helium 1.083$μ$m triplet, a reduction that is fairly uniform across the line. The Orion Nebula is a blister HII region, with a dense, bright ionised layer on the far side from the observer near the Orion A molecular cloud and lower density gas elsewhere. Using a simple radiative transfer model, we show that dark features arise when emission from the dense layer is absorbed by intermediate density helium (e.g. in clumps, globules, or winds from objects like proplyds) on the near side of the dense layer.

title: The MAGPI Survey: the evolution of galaxy spin-filament alignments since z~0.3
abstract: We present measurements of galaxy spin-filament alignments at 0.20<z<0.42 using the MAGPI Survey, exploiting resolved stellar and ionised gas kinematics to reconstruct 3D spin axes. Cosmic filaments are identified using a stellar mass-matched constant-number-density population from the GAMA, MAGPI Redshift Survey and DESI datasets. We detect a flipping of the statistical alignment signal at z~0.3 as a function of M*: low-mass galaxies preferentially exhibit spins parallel to the direction of their host filaments, while high-mass galaxies tend towards perpendicular orientations. The transition mass is measured to be log(M{*,t}/Msun)~10.8, approximately 0.6 dex higher than the value for the SAMI Galaxy Survey at z~0.05. Bootstrap analysis gives 99.5% confidence that the transition mass is higher for MAGPI than SAMI. At fixed stellar mass MAGPI galaxies exhibit stronger parallel alignments than their SAMI counterparts, suggesting evolution of spin-filament alignments over the past ~3 Gyr. The gaseous component in MAGPI galaxies is more closely aligned with filaments than the stellar component, relative to a M*-matched SAMI sample. This indicates a stronger coupling between ionised gas and the large-scale structure at z~0.3, consistent with coherent gas accretion onto filaments remaining efficient at higher M*. At z~0 we detect a transition toward perpendicular alignments at lower M*, while the gas and stellar components exhibit similar alignments relative to filaments, likely due to the cumulative effects of mergers and secular evolution.

title: Dust-induced reversal of the optical wavelength dependence of spiral-arm pitch angles
abstract: The classical density-wave scenario predicts a blue-to-red age--colour gradient across the spiral arms of disc galaxies as a consequence of shock-induced star formation. However, observations of spiral-arm pitch angles at different wavelengths sometimes suggest the opposite trend, namely a red-to-blue ``colour jump''. The origin of this apparent contradiction remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the effects of dust attenuation on post-shock stellar emission, together with the streamline motions of gas and stellar populations. We find that dust attenuation in regions with relatively high optical depths, $\hatτ_{V} \gtrsim 0.2$, can produce an apparent red-to-blue spatial sequence, with respect to the shock location, by reversing the relative positions of the flux maxima of stellar populations observed in different bands. Moreover, streamline motions confine post-shock stellar populations near the spiral arms for longer than in a circular-orbit model, thereby modifying the spatial distribution of the emitted light. We conclude that the apparent red-to-blue colour jump does not necessarily contradict the classical density-wave scenario. Instead, it can arise from the same post-shock stellar populations that intrinsically produce a blue-to-red age--colour gradient if their emission is modified by dust attenuation.

title: Intranight optical monitoring of eight quasars with superluminal jets and low optical polarization: Probing the mechanism of rapid flux variability
abstract: Intranight optical variability (INOV) of blazars whose emission arises predominantly from a relativistic jet, has been widely linked to a combination of two key observational diagnostics: the fractional optical polarization ($P_{opt}$) and the Doppler boost arising from relativistic beaming of the jet's emission. To discern which of these two factors plays the dominant role, we investigate INOV of a well-defined representative sample of 8 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs, which are `low-synchrotron-peaked' blazars) whose jets exhibit a low degree of polarization ($P_{opt}$ < 3$\%$) but a large superluminal motion with c$β_{app}$ = 5c $-$ 31c (median = 10c). We report sensitive optical monitoring of these 8 `low-polarization superluminal quasars' (LPSQs) using a 1.3-metre telescope, in 20 sessions of minimum 3-hour duration. These data were supplemented with similarly high-quality monitoring data/results available in the literature for this sample, thus adding another 19 sessions. Duty cycle (DC) of strong INOV (amplitude $ψ> 5\%$) is found to be zero, applying the normally used $F_η$ test, and $\sim 7\%$ using the more powerful `enhanced $F$-test'. The small DC, despite the strong Doppler boost expected from the observed high superluminality, shows that strong INOV is much rarer among LPSQs, compared to high-polarization quasars, for which DC $(ψ> 5\%$) is found to be around 30%, even using the $F_η$ test. This provides the first compelling evidence that optical polarization is the primary diagnostic of INOV, while relativistic beaming plays a supportive role. Possible implications for the proposed mechanisms for INOV are pointed out.

title: A Supermagnified Little Red Dot with a Resolved Host
abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are an intriguing new class of sources in the early universe discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) characterized by V-shaped spectra and extremely compact sizes. Their underlying mechanisms still remain the subject of ongoing debate. We present JWST observations of a gravitationally lensed LRD nicknamed "Best Friend" at $z_{\rm spec} = 8.297\pm0.002$. Its high magnification factor of $μ= 36^{+8}_{-12}$ makes it the highest magnified LRD reported to date and unveils both the resolved structure of its host and a central engine less than 7 pc in size. The spectrum of the central engine, in which broad lines are not detected, possibly owing to the limited S/N and spectral resolution, is better interpreted as black hole activity rather than a dense star cluster. The latter cannot be fully excluded, but if true, the resulting lower limit on stellar density would be $>1.25^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\cdot10^6 \mathrm{M_{\odot}/pc}^2$, which is around 2 orders of magnitude higher than stellar densities of typical clusters at high-z. By performing a spatially resolved analysis of NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy, we find that the host stellar mass is $\log(M_\star/M_{\odot}) = 7.3^{+0.2}_{-0.8}$. Best Friend demonstrates the power of lensing to reveal the morphologies of LRDs.

title: Hidden Neutrino Active Galaxy Candidates: Prospects for Catalog and Stacking Searches with IceCube, IceCube-Gen2, and KM3NeT
abstract: In high-energy neutrino astrophysics, the identification of high-energy neutrino sources is a central goal, and jet-quiet active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have emerged as promising candidates. For this purpose, we present a theory-guided, intrinsic X-ray selected sample of hidden neutrino AGN candidates consisting of $28$ X-ray bright AGNs (X-HiNAC), combining the {\em Swift}/BAT and BASS surveys with dedicated {\em NuSTAR} observations and spectral analyses. We compile their intrinsic X-ray fluxes, spectral properties, luminosity distances, and supermassive black hole masses, to provide a coherent sample for neutrino source searches. The sample is physically motivated but remains model independent given that the neutrino flux is proportional to the intrinsic X-ray flux. Using the magnetically powered corona model, we also demonstrate the prospects for individual-source and stacking searches with IceCube-Gen2 and KM3NeT. We identify promising individual targets and find that stacking the remaining sources, excluding NGC 1068, could yield a $5σ$ detection within $\sim 5-15$ years under favorable model assumptions at the current and upcoming neutrino observatories. We highlight systematic uncertainties in the adopted source parameters, particularly the black hole masses, for which different measurement techniques can yield estimates differing by up to an order of magnitude. Such uncertainties can significantly affect the predicted neutrino emission, motivating more precise black hole mass measurements and improved broadband X-ray observations. Our findings motivate improved multiwavelength characterization of nearby AGNs and provide a guide for investigating their role as high-energy neutrino sources.

title: MARTA: A "little" black hole hidden in a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z~3.8
abstract: JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime. We report a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at $z=3.7694$, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE data. We detect a broad H$α$ component with $L_{\rm Hα,b}=2.35\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and FWHM $=1270^{+260}_{-250}$ km s$^{-1}$, with no [O III] counterpart of comparable width. Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot)=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23}$ and $λ_{\rm Edd}=0.07$, or up to 0.38 for alternative calibrations. The host comprises at least three compact clumps, with $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$. If stellar photoionization dominates the narrow lines, the gas is highly ionized and metal poor, with $12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm0.04$ ($\simeq0.10\,Z_\odot$). The inferred $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star=2.3\%$ lies about 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed host. If growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ($t_{10}=92$ Myr ago), a $10^2\,M_\odot$ seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio $\simeq5.7$; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse, seed would allow sub-Eddington mean accretion. MUSE reveals extended Ly$α$ emission ($\simeq6.5$-6.9 proper kpc), offset by $+64^{+10}_{-8}$ km s$^{-1}$ from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of $\simeq0.44$. Together with a Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O III]/[O II] ratio, this makes MARTA 3887 a laboratory to study black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape jointly.

title: EMBER: A Little Red Dot Candidate at $z_{\rm spec}=10.36$ in the Seed Black Hole Era
abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are a newly discovered population that may trace rapidly growing black holes (BHs) and provide a link between seed BHs and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGNs). However, no LRD had previously been spectroscopically confirmed at $z>10$, leaving this earliest phase observationally unexplored. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the EMBER program, we measure a spectroscopic redshift of $z_{\rm spec}=10.361^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$ for \target, the highest-redshift LRD candidate known to date. The redshift is constrained by a prominent Ly$α$ break and multiple tentative emission lines, including C\,{\sc iv}\,$λ\lambda1549,1551$ and [O\,{\sc iii}]\,$\lambda4363$ detected at $S/N=3.9$ and $3.6$, respectively. Its extreme NIRCam-MIRI color of $m_{\rm F444W}-m_{\rm F770W}=1.82\pm0.1$, characteristic V-shaped continuum with a turnover near the Balmer limit, and continuum slopes of $β_{\rm UV}=-2.26^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and $β_{\rm opt}=1.17^{+0.74}_{-0.70}$ all support its LRD nature. A possible iron complex at $λ_{\rm rest}\sim0.24$--$0.25\,{\rm μm}$ and a possibly high $\log\left([{\rm O\,III]\,\lambda4363/\rm Hγ}\right)=0.17^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$ further support an AGN-like interpretation, as seen in previously known LRDs. Tentative detection of Ly$α$ emission may indicate enhanced Ly$α$ transmission at $z\sim10$. Our findings extend the observational frontier of BH growth into the seed-BH formation era, and upcoming MIRI spectroscopy will further establish the physical nature of the source.

title: Developing Environments: Formation and Quenching at Cosmic Noon Traced by the Large-scale Distribution of Gas and Galaxies
abstract: Environmental density correlates with galaxy properties in the local Universe, but how and when these trends emerge is unclear: at cosmic noon, large-scale structures are still assembling and galaxies quench rapidly for debated reasons. We study how the formation and quenching histories of massive galaxies at $1.7<z<3.5$ depend on environment, using two independent tracers: galaxy number density ($δ_\#$) from COSMOS-Web and intergalactic neutral hydrogen ($δ_{HI}$, cool gas) from LATIS Ly$α$ tomography. We combine 139 Blue Jay JWST/NIRSpec galaxies with 57 DAWN JWST Archive prism spectra in COSMOS, deriving stellar masses, star formation histories, dust attenuation, and Na\,{\sc d} outflow rates from joint spectro-photometric \texttt{Prospector} fits. In massive quiescent galaxies, the formation-to-quenching interval increases with density. AGN and Na\,{\sc d} outflows are confined to $δ_\#<0.5$ and elevated Ly$α$ absorption ($δ_{HI}>1$), mostly in massive quiescent galaxies showing both. About 65\% of the sample follows a correlation between the tracers; two outlier regions stand out. A galaxy-rich, gas-poor region ($δ_\#>2$, $δ_{HI}<1$) coincides with one of the most massive Hyperion protocluster cores, where the gas is plausibly fully ionized; its quiescent galaxies formed earlier and lack significant AGN activity and outflows. A galaxy-poor, gas-rich region ($δ_\#<1$, $δ_{HI}>1$), within 60 cMpc of the densest Hyperion cores, hosts rapidly quenched galaxies with a high incidence of AGN and outflows. This \emph{developing environment}, distinct from both mature protoclusters and the field, likely traces massive halos still assembling. Galaxy counts alone cannot capture the environment at cosmic noon: jointly mapping galaxies and cool gas is crucial to understand how environment regulates gas accretion, star formation, and quenching.

title: Formation of Micron-sized Presolar Graphite Grains in Low-energy Supernova Ejecta
abstract: Presolar graphite grains with supernova isotopic signatures provide direct evidence that large graphite grains formed in supernova ejecta. However, theoretical calculations of dust formation in supernovae have typically predicted graphite grains smaller than $0.1\,{\rm μm}$, leaving unclear the physical conditions required to form those grains with radii of order $1\,{\rm μm}$. We systematically investigate graphite nucleation and growth in expanding supernova ejecta by varying the explosion energy, ejecta mass, initial ejecta radius, and ejected $^{56}$Ni mass. We use a simplified one-zone model that follows the temperature and density evolution including adiabatic cooling, radiative cooling, and heating by radioactive nickel. We show that the final graphite grain size is mainly determined by the product of the mass density of atomic carbon available for grain growth and the local cooling timescale, both evaluated at a reference temperature of $2000\,{\rm K}$. Our models show that graphite growth is favored by lower explosion energy, larger ejecta mass, and smaller initial ejecta radius, which keep the gas denser near the graphite-condensation temperature. When radioactive heating and radiative cooling are included, explosions with $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{50}\,{\rm erg}$ and $M_{\rm Ni}\lesssim10^{-3}\,M_\odot$ can form $1$-$10\,μ{\rm m}$ graphite grains in the ejected helium layer or carbon-oxygen core, whereas $E_{\rm exp}\sim10^{51}\,{\rm erg}$ models do not. These results suggest that micron-sized presolar supernova graphite preferentially forms in faint-supernova-like explosions with low explosion energies, little ejected nickel, and helium layer or carbon-oxygen core ejecta.

title: Stellar Kinematics and Molecular Gas toward NGC 6357: An Overlooked Earlier Stellar Generation
abstract: We investigate past star formation in NGC 6357 using Gaia DR3 astrometry and Three-mm Ultimate Mopra Milky Way Survey (ThrUMMS) $^{12}$CO($J=1$--0) data. A Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) search independently recovers the previously cataloged cluster G352.8+0.6 in addition to Pismis 24, G353.1+0.6, and G353.2+0.6. Isochrone fitting yields an age of $7.9^{+1.5}_{-1.4}$ Myr for G352.8+0.6, compared with approximately 1--3 Myr for the three young clusters. Assuming constant relative plane-of-sky motion, a linear traceback places G352.8+0.6 closest to their reference center approximately 1.8 Myr ago, comparable to their inferred ages. The $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ CO component overlaps G352.8+0.6 in projection and shows localized depressions in integrated intensity around three spectroscopically identified massive stars belonging to G352.8+0.6. The $-4$ and $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ components show complementary projected distributions and intermediate-velocity CO emission in position--velocity space. Assuming that the $+2$ km s$^{-1}$ component was physically associated with G352.8+0.6 and shared its transverse motion, our principal interpretation is that the two molecular structures interacted around the epoch indicated by the stellar traceback, approximately 1.8 Myr ago. The resulting gas compression may have contributed to the recent episode of clustered and high-mass star formation in NGC 6357 and to the formation of Shell A, which subsequent stellar feedback may have reshaped.

title: The 943 MHz radio-SFR relation of nearby galaxies observed with ASKAP
abstract: We investigate the integrated 943 MHz radio-infrared and radio-star-formation-rate (SFR) relations of 875 nearby galaxies within $D<50$ Mpc using public Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP) observations. After excluding galaxies with identified or candidate AGN activity, 594 galaxies remain in the AGN-cleaned sample. We used Bayesian errors-in-variables models that account for measurement uncertainties, intrinsic scatter, and correlated distance errors. The AGN-cleaned radio-infrared relation is nearly linear, $L_{ν,943}\propto L_{ν,\mathrm{W4}}^{1.09\pm0.02}$, with an orthogonal intrinsic scatter of $0.21\pm0.01$ dex, and is tighter than the AGN-host relation. For 592 AGN-cleaned galaxies, the radio-SFR relation is approximately linear, $L_{ν,943}\propto{\rm SFR}^{1.02\pm0.02}$, with an intrinsic scatter of $0.25\pm0.01$ dex. Semi-calorimetric models reveal positive secondary dependences on stellar mass, $γ=0.09\pm0.03$, and rotation velocity, $δ=0.24\pm0.08$. The consistency between these two secondary trends suggests that the galaxy gravitational potential may weakly regulate CRE confinement and synchrotron-radiation efficiency. Our results provide an integrated 943 MHz radio-SFR calibration for nearby galaxies and show that, although radio luminosity scales nearly proportionally with SFR on average, weak secondary dependences on galaxy properties remain.

title: Collisional excitation of HMgC$_3$N by He: rate coefficients and astrophysical implications
abstract: Reliable collisional data are essential for interpreting the rotational emission of HMgC$_3$N under the non-equilibrium conditions of molecular clouds. We investigate the rotational excitation and de-excitation of HMgC$_3$N induced by collisions with He, combining \textit{ab initio} calculations with quantum scattering theory. A two-dimensional potential energy surface (PES) for HMgC$_3$N--He was constructed using the CCSD(T)-F12A method in conjunction with the aug-cc-pVTZ basis set. Quantum close-coupling (CC) calculation were then performed to obtain state-to-state integral cross sections and temperature-dependent rate coefficients for rotational transitions with $Δj=\pm1$, $\pm2$, and $\pm3$, covering rotational levels up to $j=20$ and temperatures from $3$ to $50$~K. The rate coefficients exhibit a clear propensity for $Δj=\pm2$ transitions. The resulting collisional data were incorporated into radiative transfer modelling to constrain the physical conditions and column density of HMgC$_3$N from its observed spectral line emission. A $χ^2$ minimization yields a best-fitting H$_2$ volume density of $n(\mathrm{H}_2)=1.233\times10^5~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$ and column density of $N(\mathrm{HMgC}_3\mathrm{N})=1.831\times10^{12}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. The derived column density is in approximate agreement with the observational estimate of $(3.0\pm0.6)\times10^{12}~\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$. These results provide new collisional data for non-LTE studies of HMgC$_3$N and support a more realistic treatment of its rotational excitation and radiative transfer in molecular clouds.

title: Bar likelihood in local galaxies: the joint role of stellar mass, morphology and environment
abstract: We investigate how the likelihood of hosting a stellar bar depends on both intrinsic galaxy properties and environment, using a volume-limited sample of central and satellite galaxies from the NASA-Sloan Atlas, spanning isolated systems, low- and high-richness groups, and massive haloes, complemented with halo-based environmental information and probabilistic morphology. Using probabilistic bar identification, we quantify the bar likelihood as a function of stellar mass, colour, morphology, halo mass, and cluster-centric distance. We find that stellar mass and morphology are the galaxy properties most associated with the bar likelihood. At fixed morphology, the probability of hosting a bar increases with stellar mass, particularly for late-type galaxies. At the same time, morphology strongly modulates the overall incidence of bars, with early-type galaxies displaying systematically lower probabilities than late-type systems across the stellar mass range. Environmental trends are observed, including halo mass and cluster-centric distance, but these trends largely reflect the morphological composition of the galaxy population. In particular, the decrease in bar likelihood towards the centres of massive haloes reflects the increasing fraction of early-type galaxies, consistent with the morphology-density relation, rather than a direct environmental suppression of bars. Our residual analysis finds no statistically significant residual dependence on halo mass or normalized cluster-centric distance after accounting for stellar mass and morphology, within the sensitivity of this sample. Overall, our results show that stellar mass and morphology are the main factors associated with bar likelihood.

title: The multiple origins of spurs in stellar streams: a challenge for dark matter diagnostics
abstract: Spurs along stellar streams are often interpreted as signatures of interactions with dark matter subhalos, and thus have been proposed as diagnostics on the clustering and nature of dark matter. Although galactic baryonic components could play similar roles as gravitational perturbers of streams, the possible signatures they leave and the degeneracy with subhalos have been overlooked. In this paper, we analyse simulations of streams experiencing disruptions by dark matter subhalos, a galactic bar, and a galaxy merger. Although spurs are more frequently found to be induced by the galaxy merger, the spurs originating from all these processes are morphologically similar. Therefore, such morphological features should not be used alone to characterise the mechanism of their origin, nor to constrain the nature of dark matter.

title: The Pristine Survey. XXX. Mapping substructures in the inner and outer halo with blue horizontal branch stars
abstract: Blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars serve as good standard candles and kinematic tracers of the Milky Way halo. The halo displays various overdensities and kinematical substructures of different shapes and sizes. Our objective is to investigate the substructure in three dimensions and the bulk motion of the halo up to distances well exceeding the limit of the Gaia parallaxes. We selected BHB stars in the $\left(u-CaHK\right) _ 0$-$(g-r) _ 0$ colour-colour diagram with a hierarchical Bayesian mixture model of three populations: BHB stars, blue straggler stars, and outliers. Using $CaHK$ photometry derived from Gaia XP spectra and the Pristine survey, we provide both a shallow and a deep catalogue of BHB stars of 7,057 and 8,824 stars, respectively, where the deep catalogue is restricted to the deeper Pristine footprint compared to the shallower with Gaia XP. Using the shallow catalogue, we trace to larger distances 6D substructures identified earlier within a 2.5 kpc from the Sun, including accepted populations; namely, Gaia-Enceladus, Thamnos, Helmi streams, Sequoia, and other smaller halo substructures such as ED-3, ED-4, and ED-6. The deep catalogue provides reliable distance measurements for a more detailed 3D mapping of the Sagittarius stream and of the Pisces Overdensity. We add new candidate BHB stars with line-of-sight velocities to existing catalogues and confirm previously reported differences between the northern and southern Galactic hemispheres, likely due to the infall of the Large Magellanic Cloud. This research demonstrates that probabilistic photometric classification can effectively identify distant candidate BHB stars, and can provide catalogues of these stars that enhance our understanding of the 3D and 6D structures in the halo of the Milky Way.

title: The Evolution of the Circumgalactic Medium after a starburst in DESI Post-Starburst Galaxies
abstract: We present a statistical study of the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) around massive post-starburst galaxies, traced by Mg II $λ\lambda2796,2803$ absorption in background quasar spectra from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Data Release 2. Cross-matching ~1.98 million quasar sightlines with luminous red galaxies at $0.4 < z < 0.76$ with stellar masses between $10.6 < \log_{10}(M_*/\mathrm{M}_\odot) < 12$ yields ~143 million galaxy-quasar pairs, 50-60 times more per impact-parameter bin than our previous SDSS-based analysis. We stack the Mg II absorption as a function of projected separation and classify the foreground galaxies using mean-field independent component analysis (MFICA), further subdividing the post-starburst population into sub-samples ordered by time since the starburst. The mean Mg II equivalent width declines with impact parameter for every class. Post-starburst galaxies show the strongest absorption of any spectral class, reaching $W_{\rm MgII} = 1.58 \pm 0.32$ Å within 71 kpc, well above star-forming ($0.69 \pm 0.15$ Å) and quiescent ($0.22 \pm 0.05$ Å) galaxies of comparable stellar mass at the same projected separation. Within the post-starburst phase the absorption profile evolves systematically: the youngest systems show the highest, most centrally concentrated absorption and the steepest radial decline, whereas progressively older systems show weaker inner absorption and enhanced absorption at intermediate radii (~300-1000 kpc). Independent Bagpipes star-formation-history fitting confirms that this ordering corresponds to an ageing sequence. We interpret this evolution as the outward redistribution of cool gas expelled by feedback-driven winds, consistent with characteristic outflow velocities of a few hundred km s$^{-1}$, with a residual inner cool-gas reservoir persisting throughout the post-starburst phase.

title: The Broad-Line Region Size-Luminosity Relation in AGN Constrained by the Viewing Angle with the FRADO Model
abstract: We investigate the H$β$ broad-line region (BLR) size-luminosity ($R_{\rm BLR}$-$L_{5100}$) relation of active galactic nuclei (AGN) using a Bayesian viewing angle inference framework based on the Failed Radiatively Accelerated Dusty Outflow (FRADO) model. First, we update the FRADO model by introducing a phase factor to account for the anisotropic visibility of the illuminated cloud surface. Second, we construct a Bayesian framework to constrain the viewing angle by matching the FRADO-based $R_{\rm BLR}$ to the measured H$β$ lags of 151 AGN from Wang & Woo (2024). We successfully reproduce the slope and intrinsic scatter of the observed $R_{\rm BLR}$-$L_{5100}$ relation, finding that the inferred viewing angles are broadly consistent with the estimates from dynamical modeling of velocity-resolved reverberation data, albeit with substantial scatter. As the observed H$β$ time lag and line velocity depend on the viewing angle, the black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$) calibrated from our work is typically larger than the reverberation-mapping estimates using an average virial factor. Our results provide a physically motivated interpretation of the $R_{\rm BLR}$-$L_{5100}$ relation and the systematic uncertainties in reverberation and single-epoch $M_{\rm BH}$ estimates.

title: Co-evolution of AGN and Host Galaxies across Cosmic Time Using JWST data
abstract: Understanding the complex co-evolution of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and their host galaxies across cosmic time remains a fundamental challenge, particularly in identifying how the physical drivers of galaxy diversity evolve from the early Universe to the present day. To understand this, we use a multi-wavelength JWST catalog of 2,709 sources cross-matched from the SMILES and JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) surveys, spanning lookback times from 0.8 to 12.9 Gyr ($0.05 <z <6$). Using Pearson correlation matrix, we find AGN luminosity ($L_{\mathrm{AGN}}$) strongly correlates ($\sim0.8$) with star formation rate (SFR) and dust luminosity ($L_{\mathrm{dust}}$), weakly correlates ($\sim0.5$) with stellar mass ($M_\star$) and anti-correlates ($\sim -0.4$) with star formation history (SFH) duration and stellar age (Age$_\star$). However, the apparent anti-correlation observed between galaxy age and AGN luminosity is driven by cosmic time rather than by a direct physical connection. Using Principal Component Analysis (PCA), we find that galaxy diversity is fundamentally governed by two principal components: AGN and galaxy activity, and stellar age. At higher redshifts, AGN accretion, star formation, and dust emission are tightly synchronized, reflecting gas-rich conditions in the early Universe. In contrast, the present Universe exhibits a clear bimodal structure in host-dominated systems ($f_{\mathrm{AGN}} \leq 0.2$), separating quiescent and star-forming galaxies. Our results demonstrate that AGN luminosity is primarily governed by the host galaxy's current cold-gas supply, of which recent star formation is a close observational tracer, with galaxy mass setting the overall potential. This highlights a co-evolution scenario in which black hole growth and star formation are tightly linked, particularly at early cosmic epochs.

title: The JWST/PASSAGE Survey: Metallicity Radial Gradients in Emission-Line Galaxy Pairs at Cosmic Noon with NIRISS
abstract: Using JWST/NIRISS slitless spectroscopy from the PASSAGE program, we analyze 17 spectroscopically confirmed emission-line galaxies in candidate interacting systems at $z \sim 1.7$--$3.2$. These galaxies span stellar masses of $7.3 \lesssim \log(M_*/M_\odot) \lesssim 10.4$ and global gas-phase metallicities of $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H}) \sim 7.6$--$8.7$. From spatially resolved emission-line maps, we measure radial metallicity gradients separately for each galaxy, finding values from approximately $-0.2$ to $+0.45$ dex kpc$^{-1}$. The mean metallicity gradients in bins of stellar mass and redshift are consistent with previous measurements, and their scatter is not significantly different from that of the heterogeneous literature compilation in either the metallicity-gradient--stellar-mass or metallicity-gradient--redshift relation. We find tentative evidence for an anti-correlation between the metallicity gradient and the metallicity offset from the mass--metallicity relation, with a best-fit slope of $-0.30 \pm 0.06$, possibly reflecting interaction-driven variations in star formation and chemical enrichment. Galaxies in pairs with comparable component masses tend to exhibit positive metallicity gradients, whereas galaxies in unequal-mass pairs tend to exhibit negative gradients; neither trend is statistically significant in the present sample. Overall, our results reveal substantial diversity in the metallicity distributions of candidate interacting systems at cosmic noon and provide tentative evidence that galaxy interactions may influence the redistribution of gas and metals.

title: Dark Halos, Intermediate-Mass BH and Nuclear Stellar Clusters in Dwarf Spheroidals
abstract: We exploit the halo densities of three dwarf spheroidals recently obtained to investigate their dark matter distribution. We address the well-known DM halo core-cusp issue by finding that the NFW $Λ$CDM halo profile is in strong disagreement with these inferred halo densities, which instead result very well-reproduced by the Burkert halo cored profile with the central density $ρ_0$ and the core radius $r_0$. These structural parameters result connected among themselves and with the length scale of the stellar matter component in a way similar to that present in disk systems. By analyzing the properties of dark halo densities in their innermost regions, we find no trace of a central intermediate-mass black hole or of a nuclear stellar cluster.

title: As a matter of reconstruction -- varying the magnetic Prandtl number in implicit large eddy simulations
abstract: The magnetic Prandtl number ($\mathrm{Pm}$), the ratio of viscosity to magnetic diffusivity, spans many orders of magnitude in astrophysical plasmas. It shapes how turbulence amplifies and structures magnetic fields. In direct numerical simulations (DNS) the viscosity and magnetic diffusivity can be controlled explicitly and independently, whereas in implicit large eddy simulations (ILES) they are set by the numerical scheme. We test whether, in a finite-volume code, $\mathrm{Pm}$ can be varied through the reconstruction scheme by applying different methods to the hydro and magnetic variables. As a proof of concept, we simulate driven, subsonic, homogeneous magnetohydrodynamic turbulence using five pairs of hydrodynamic and magnetic reconstruction schemes at varying resolutions. We measure the effective viscosity and resistivity from the energy transfer between scales. Reconstructing the magnetic field at higher order than the fluid raises the effective magnetic Prandtl number and vice versa. We demonstrate that a mix of second- and third-order reconstruction alone results in a $\gtrsim20\times$ change in $\mathrm{Pm}$. A comparison of DNS with matched explicit dissipation at these values agrees with the ILES. Mixed reconstruction thus offers a simple and efficient way to explore $\mathrm{Pm} \not\simeq 1$ in ILES without adding explicit dissipation.

title: OASIS III: Bursty star formation drives observed galaxy sizes at $z\geq4$
abstract: We employ JWST/NIRSpec MSA PRISM spectroscopy together with NIRCam imaging to investigate the impact of star-formation variability on galaxy sizes for a representative sample of 51 galaxies at $z\geq4$. The OASIS survey enables us to probe low-star-formation-rate (SFR) lulling and mini-quenched galaxies down to $\log_{10}(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.3$ and $\log_{10}(\mathrm{SFR}/M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1})<-1.6$, i.e. more than one order of magnitude below the star-forming main sequence (MS). This enables us to probe objects that are often missed by shallower spectroscopic surveys, in addition to the MS and starburst systems, yielding an SFR- and mass-representative sample at high redshift. We derive galaxy half-light sizes using ForcePho, enabling us to resolve the highly compact nature of these sources, and we analyse their star-formation histories and interstellar medium (ISM) properties with the full-spectral-fitting code ppxf. We find a clear anti-correlation between burstiness, as traced by the ratio of the SFR from H$α$ compared to that from non-parametric spectral fitting averaged over 100 Myr, and galaxy UV/optical half-light radii as measured with ForcePho from a combination of well-sampled NIRCam photometry. Using partial correlation coefficients we show that the anti-correlation between burstiness (as traced by the SFR ratio) and size cannot simply be explained by secondary dependencies on stellar mass or redshift. We interpret this relation as the effect of central starbursts in SFR-rising (bursting) systems, where intense central star formation reduces measured galaxy half-light sizes. This burstiness then regulates galaxy sizes at high redshift. Should the same mechanism be present at $z>10$, this could explain the size bimodality seen in the UV luminous galaxies as simply stemming from a more fundamental relationship between burstiness and size.

title: OASIS II: The Ionized Gas Traces Feedback-Driven Declines into the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
abstract: Models of bursty star formation in low-mass (10^8-10^9.5 Msun) galaxies at z>4 differ most in the suppressed phases: what drives the decline, how fast star formation falls, and how long it stays low. OASIS Paper I showed that such quiet galaxies are common and old; here we measure how they got there and how their ionized gas responds. We compare Balmer-line star-formation rates (SFRs) with 100-Myr averages from the stellar continuum, in NIRSpec/PRISM spectra of 54 OASIS galaxies at z>4, including three mini-quenched galaxies below the quenching threshold and five lulling galaxies at least 0.6 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) but still star-forming. Galaxies above the SFMS rise and fade equally often, whereas those below it are mostly fading: the lulling galaxies formed little more than a tenth of their mass in the last 100 Myr, and their decline began tens to ~100 Myr before observation. Suppressed phases thus last of order 100 Myr, as long as or longer than in most simulations, whereas recovery is much faster: few galaxies below the SFMS are rising. The ionized gas tracks these changes in star formation. [OIII]/[OII] falls from galaxies above the SFMS to the lulling ones, even at fixed mass and after dust correction, and follows the recent change in SFR (SFR_10/SFR_100) more closely than the position relative to the SFMS: two rising galaxies below the SFMS are highly ionized. This is expected if fewer and softer ionizing photons than in strongly star-forming galaxies meet gas depleted by earlier star formation. Lulling galaxies show ISM conditions distinct from those of strongly star-forming galaxies. The declines are faster than passive gas exhaustion predicts, favoring feedback that expels the gas or keeps it from forming stars. Quiet phases are thus long, feedback-driven episodes, and the ionized gas traces where a galaxy is in its burst cycle.

title: OASIS I: Spectroscopy of Mini-Quenched and Lulling Galaxies Constrains the Quiet Side of Bursty Star Formation at z > 4
abstract: JWST has revealed that star formation in early galaxies is bursty, including episodes of violent suppression, so-called mini-quenching. But these were largely serendipitous discoveries in samples of UV-bright, emission-line-dominated galaxies, so that the quiet side of the burst cycle has remained poorly explored. With the JWST Cycle 3 program OASIS (GO 5997), we searched for such galaxies deliberately, using deep 28-hour NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy across the full burst cycle at z>4. We identify three mini-quenched galaxies with log(M*/Msun) = 8.3-8.9 and no detectable Balmer emission, at least 1.2-1.7 dex below the star-forming main sequence (SFMS), five lulling galaxies with weak Balmer emission above the quenching threshold, and 17 nearly-main-sequence galaxies just below the SFMS. Finding them required spectroscopy: seven of our ten photometric candidates for suppressed (mini-quenched and lulling) galaxies turned out to be nearly-MS or above the SFMS, and photometric fits overestimate their current star-formation rates and cannot distinguish lulling from mini-quenched ones. The suppressed galaxies are common: five of the eight come from tiers not selected on star-formation state, where they make up 29% of the galaxies at z = 4-5.5 and log(M*/Msun) = 8-9.5, a number density of ~1.6x10^-3 Mpc^-3 dex^-1. Simulations predict them to be an order of magnitude rarer at these masses and to occur mainly at lower masses. The suppressed galaxies are also old: Balmer-break strength and stellar age both increase as galaxies fall further below the SFMS, with light-weighted ages of 5 Myr for galaxies above it, ~30 Myr for the lulling galaxies and above 100 Myr for the mini-quenched ones. They show little stellar reddening (E(B-V) < 0.2), consistent with depleted gas reservoirs. Suppressed phases at z>4 are therefore neither rare nor brief, but a common and lasting part of early galaxy growth.

title: Resolving the Complex Line-Locking Structure in Quasar J004613+010425 with VLT/X-shooter Spectroscopy
abstract: Line-locking (LL) signatures in quasar absorption-line systems provide direct observational evidence for radiatively driven outflows. We present a detailed investigation of LL phenomena in the quasar SDSS J004613.54+010425.7 ($z_{\rm em} = 2.150$) using medium-resolution VLT/X-shooter spectra, as part of the TOLL project. Compared with previous studies based on Sloan Digital Sky Survey spectroscopy, the X-shooter data resolve the absorption complex into twelve narrow absorption line (NAL) components spanning $\sim$$2700$ km/s in the C IV, N V, Si IV, and Ly$α$ transitions, a factor of $\sim$2.4 more components than identified from lower resolution spectra. We detect fourteen distinct LL pairs across three ionic species, forming one of the largest line-locking webs known to date: three Si IV pairs connecting components (2, 10), (4, 11), and (5, 12); six N V pairs organized into four groups; and five C IV pairs organized into three groups. Monte Carlo simulations show that the probability of this twelve-component LL web arising by chance is $< 10^{-5}$. Photoionization modeling with Cloudy yields ionization parameters of $\log U \approx -2.4$ to $-0.6$ and total hydrogen column densities of $\log N({\rm H}) \approx 18.4$-$20.6$ for the twelve components. A comparison of the properties of shadowed and shadowing clouds shows that ion column densities and ionization parameters typically agree within a factor of $\sim$3, broadly supporting the standard radiative acceleration picture, although several outliers suggest that multi-ion locking and cloud-cloud interactions may also regulate LL stability. These results demonstrate that medium- and high-resolution spectroscopy is essential for resolving the full complexity of line-locked quasar outflows.

title: Kinematic Map of the Galactic Bulge Using HST Proper Motions
abstract: Constraining the Galactic bulge's non-axisymmetric dynamics requires proper motions in deep fields across many sightlines, yet crowding and extinction limit such measurements. Using multi-epoch observations of 27 fields in the southern Galactic bulge (-6$^\circ$ < l < 4$^\circ$, -5$^\circ$ < b < -1$^\circ$) from the ultraviolet-visible (UVIS) channel of Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) on the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) with time baselines of 3 to 13 years, and combining them with the absolute proper motion reference frame provided by Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3), we measure absolute proper motions for ~ 400,000 stars. Colour-magnitude diagrams are used to separate bulge stars from foreground disc stars, identify red clump stars and correct for interstellar extinction and reddening. Statistical analysis shows that the mean proper motion in Galactic latitude is consistent with that of the central supermassive black hole Sgr A*, while the mean proper motion in Galactic longitude is affected by disc stars but agrees with Sgr A* after extrapolation to the Galactic plane. Proper motion dispersions increase towards the Galactic centre and are asymmetric across Galactic longitude, with a steeper gradient for l < 0$^\circ$, revealing the bulge's non-axisymmetric bar structure. The velocity distribution shows clear anisotropy ($σ_l$/$σ_b$ = 1.131 $\pm$ 0.005). The normalised covariance is negative in the l > 0$^\circ$ region (~ -0.085) and close to zero in the l < 0$^\circ$ region. The proper motion distributions are non-Gaussian in both Galactic longitude and latitude, mainly due to contamination by foreground disc stars.

title: Stellar Bars Reshape the Spatial Distribution of UV-bright Clumps in Nearby Galaxies
abstract: Stellar bars redistribute gas and angular momentum in disk galaxies, but whether they mainly change the amount or the spatial organization of recent star formation remains uncertain. We use archival HST/WFC3 F275W imaging to study 70 barred galaxies and 95 unbarred control galaxies matched in stellar mass, optical color, redshift, and F275W background noise. A uniform dendrogram-based procedure identifies 95,486 UV-bright star-forming clumps. We compare their radial and azimuthal distributions, central F275W emission, and luminosity and size distribution functions. Relative to their controls, barred galaxies show a deficit of clumps at intermediate radii broadly corresponding to the bar region, followed by a local recovery near the bar ends. Their clumps are also preferentially concentrated along the bar major axis. These spatial differences are stronger in high-mass galaxies. Normalized bar length is more closely associated with the radial redistribution and central F275W concentration than bar ellipticity, although its relation to the azimuthal distribution is less uniform. When galactocentric radius is normalized by bar length, the recovery occurs near $R/R_{\rm bar}\sim1$, indicating that the bar sets a characteristic scale for the redistribution. Despite these spatial differences, barred and control galaxies have broadly similar clump luminosity and size distribution functions. Our results suggest that stellar bars mainly reorganize where recent star formation occurs, rather than substantially altering the observed luminosities and sizes of individual UV clumps, and that this effect depends on galaxy mass and bar extent.

title: The Size-Mass Relation and Inside-Out Quenching of Massive Quiescent Galaxies at $2<z<3$ with JWST PRIMER and MINERVA
abstract: We investigate the morphology, size--mass relations, and spatially resolved star formation histories of 26 massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon ($2 < z < 3$) in the Ultra-Deep Survey field using deep JWST NIRCam imaging from the PRIMER and MINERVA surveys. Combining 16 broadband and medium-band filters with empirical point spread function matching, we perform single-Sérsic modeling and bulge--disk decompositions with pysersic across six filters (F115W to F444W), alongside Bayesian size--mass fitting with dynesty. In the rest-frame optical (F200W), the size--mass relation exhibits a steep slope of $α= 0.59 \pm 0.12$ and effective radius of $A = 0.83_{-0.07}^{+0.08}\ \mathrm{kpc}$ at $M_* = 5 \times 10^{10}\ M_\odot$. In the rest-frame near-infrared (F356W), we derive $α= 0.56 \pm 0.13$ and a more compact radius of $A = 0.70_{-0.06}^{+0.07}\ \mathrm{kpc}$. Galaxy sizes shrink by $\approx 22\%$ from F115W to F444W, reflecting negative color gradients and centrally concentrated mass profiles. Two-thirds of the sample are bulge-dominated ($B/T \ge 0.5$), whereas one-third are disk-dominated. Central bulges are ultra-compact ($R_{e,\mathrm{Bulge}} \approx 0.49\ \mathrm{kpc}$) with negligible mass dependence, whereas outer disks extend to $R_{e,\mathrm{Disk}} \approx 1.4\text{--}1.5\ \mathrm{kpc}$. Resolved spectral energy distribution modeling with piXedfit demonstrates positive radial specific star formation rate gradients and inner regions that formed at least $\approx 0.7\ \mathrm{Gyr}$ earlier and quenched faster than their outskirts. These results confirm inside-out quenching, consistent with dissipative gas compaction assembling the dense core, active galactic nucleus feedback halting central star formation, and the compact bulge dynamically stabilizing the surviving disk against fragmentation.

title: Equipartition between Alfvénic turbulence and energetic ions as the origin of the -5 common spectrum in the heliosphere
abstract: Suprathermal ion tails throughout the heliosphere follow a ``common spectrum,'' $f(v)\propto v^{-5}$. We show that scale-by-scale equipartition between strong Alfvénic turbulence and the ions it accelerates predicts both this exponent and the absolute amplitude, $F(v)=B^2/(16π^3 m_i v^5)$, with no free parameters. The prediction agrees within a factor of a few with ACE and Voyager 1 spectra across three decades in magnetic energy. We argue that this saturated level is reached where strong turbulence accelerates particles locally; quiet-time tails lie well below it, consistent with nonlocal acceleration.

title: FOMO-Z. Optimal galaxy classification, photometric redshifts, and reconstruction of population distributions
abstract: We present FOMO-Z (Flexible Optimizer of Multi-dimensional Operators and photo-$z$s), a set of statistical methods implemented in Python for galaxy classification and probabilistic inference from photometry. The methods use a reference sample with known galaxy properties. They rely on explicit, physically interpretable criteria and make no assumptions about the functional form of the color distributions. Binary selections are calibrated using either linear color conditions, particularly suited to background galaxy selection, or flexible color--color grids, seeking to maximize completeness given a threshold on purity. For probabilistic inference, the code identifies reference objects with compatible colors within photometric uncertainties to estimate each test galaxy's probability of satisfying user-defined criteria, as well as probability density functions of continuous properties such as redshift. The code also reconstructs property distributions of selected galaxy populations using photometrically similar galaxies in the reference sample. This framework supports prior weights and reference redshift probability distributions. A built-in feature-selection method identifying informative colors is also introduced. We demonstrate applications to background galaxy selection, galaxy population classification, tomographic redshift calibration, and photometric redshift estimation. The code achieves results consistent with those obtained through machine-learning approaches, such as self-organizing maps, while remaining computationally efficient, making it suitable for large photometric surveys and future Stage IV cosmological analyses. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/GiorgioLesci/FOMO-Z.

title: From Quantum Field Fluctuations to High-Redshift AGN: Semiclassical Origins of Halo Mass Function Constraints in the JWST Era
abstract: We develop a continuous framework connecting quantum field fluctuations in the early Universe to the abundance and observable properties of galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN) at cosmic dawn. Beginning with quantum fields in curved Friedmann Lemaitre Robertson Walker spacetime, we follow inflationary vacuum fluctuations into the primordial curvature spectrum, linear matter power spectrum, mass variance $σ(M,z)$, mass peak height $ν(M,z)$, and the statistics of nonlinear halo formation. The Press-Schechter and Sheth-Tormen formalisms provide an analytic description of halo abundance and its dependence on peak rarity. A complementary high redshift halo mass function calibrated with the GUREFT simulations of Yung et al. (2024) provides a numerical description specifically constructed for the cosmic dawn regime probed by JWST. The comparison between these analytic and simulation calibrated prescriptions provides a direct measure of the sensitivity of predicted halo populations to the observations. We separate this cosmological supply of halos from the astrophysical and observational mappings that produce stars, ultraviolet luminosities, and active galactic nuclei. Controlled numerical experiments show that a percent level perturbation in the primordial fluctuation amplitude produces only a modest change in $σ$ and $ν$, but can strongly amplify the exponentially suppressed high $ν$ tail of the Halo Mass Function. This sensitivity increases toward high halo mass and high redshift, identifying rare cosmic dawn populations as potentially powerful probes of primordial statistics while simultaneously exposing the importance of uncertainties in halo abundance. High redshift AGN population statistics and the Ultraviolet Luminosity Function provide additional constraints on the primordial power spectrum and dynamics of primordial inflation theory.

title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamics at z=1.7: Resolved tSZ and X-ray analysis of CL J0459.6-4946
abstract: Measurements of the entropy and temperature distribution of the intracluster medium (ICM) of local clusters have proven pivotal for the study of cluster astrophysics. Here, we extend these measurements to $z=1.7$ with a resolved analysis of the ICM in ACT/SPT-CL J0459.6-4946. By combining high-resolution thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich measurements using new, deep ALMA Band 1 and 3 observations, with archival X-ray data, we conclude that the cluster has (i) an ICM with a flat and relatively high ($\approx 200$ keV cm$^2$) entropy distribution out to $\approx 0.3\,r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, (ii) a hot core ($T_{\mathrm{e}} \simeq 14$ keV) with a declining temperature profile, (iii) a short effective path length along the line of sight of $l_{\mathrm{eff}} \simeq (0.75 \pm 0.05) \times r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, and (iv) a clumpiness factor $C = \langle n_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \rangle / \langle n_{\mathrm{e}} \rangle^2 \simeq 1.17 \pm 0.05$ within $r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$. Its dynamic nature and high redshift suggest that the cluster is still thermalising its ICM, consistent with a relatively large hydrostatic mass bias of $b = 1 - M_{500,\mathrm{c,HE}}/M_{500,\mathrm{c,WL}} = 0.27^{+0.32}_{-0.67}$ that we measure with respect to the weak lensing mass. Furthermore, a region with low entropy and high density to the south of the cluster centre is observed in the X-rays yet absent in the Compton-$y$ map, indicating pressure equilibrium; we interpret this as a sloshing cold front -- the first such detection at high redshifts. This case study demonstrates that $\approx 3$h-long ALMA observations, combined with comparatively "short" X-ray exposures ($\approx 122$ ks), can fully characterise the ICM at high redshift, opening a path towards the thermodynamics of young and distant galaxy clusters for larger samples.

title: NGDEEP: Anchoring the $0.5 < z < 3.5$ Star-Forming Main Sequence at Low Stellar Masses with Ultradeep JWST/NIRISS WFSS
abstract: Here we present deep JWST/NIRISS wide-field slitless spectroscopy (WFSS) that covers $\mathrm{Hα}$ and $\mathrm{Hβ}$ for galaxies at $0.5 < z < 3.5$ in the NGDEEP survey. The NGDEEP NIRISS observations detect emission line fluxes from galaxies in the Hubble Ultra Deep Field to $\mathrm{m_{F150W}} \lesssim$ 28 mag, enabling studies of star-formation based on $\mathrm{Hα}$ (or $\mathrm{Hβ}$, if necessary) in low-mass galaxies with $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) \gtrsim 7}$ at z = 0.5 and $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) \gtrsim 8}$ at z = 3.5. For 284 NGDEEP galaxies with $>3σ$ detections of $\mathrm{Hα}$ or $\mathrm{Hβ}$, we determine dust-corrected star-formation rates, $\mathrm{SFR_{Hα}}$, via flux measurements of these Balmer lines and compare them to the galaxies' stellar masses to investigate the properties of the star-forming main sequence (SFMS) on short, $\sim10$~Myr timescales across three redshift bins. When we contrast the intrinsic scatter in the $\mathrm{Hα}$--based SFMS to that of a SFMS comprised of UV--based SFRs, which trace star formation within the past $\sim 100$~Myr, we find that the \Ha--based SFMS's intrinsic scatter ($\approx0.35-0.5$~dex over $0.5 < z < 3.5$) is $\approx0.2-0.4$~dex higher than the UV--based SFMS's intrinsic scatter at $z < 2.5$. We argue that brief ($\lesssim10$~Myr) bursts of star formation likely account for this disparity in SFMS scatter. Theoretical predictions from the FIRE simulations underestimate the scatter we observe in the $\mathrm{Hα}$--based SFMS at $1.5 < z < 2.5$ and $\mathrm{\log(M_*/M_{\odot}) < 9}$ by up to $\approx0.25$~dex, which suggests that low-mass galaxies have burstier star-formation histories than expected on $\lesssim10$~Myr timescales.

title: Kinematic Decomposition of the BCG and ICL in Abell S1063 and MACS J1206
abstract: The brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) and the intracluster light (ICL) overlap in space and merge smoothly in surface brightness. Beyond the nearest clusters, measurements of the ICL have therefore relied on photometric definitions. We present a spectral decomposition of the light in cluster cores into BCG and ICL, using deep VLT/MUSE integral-field spectroscopy of Abell S1063 (z=0.35) and MACS J1206.2$-$0847 (z=0.44). Spectral templates of the two components are derived iteratively from the BCG center and the ICL-dominated outskirts, and their weighted sum is fitted to the spectrum of every spatial bin. This enables us to measure the kinematics and the light of the BCG and ICL separately without assuming a boundary or a functional form for their light profiles. The velocity dispersions of the BCG and ICL are $316\pm5$ and $753\pm25\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$, respectively, in AS1063, whereas we obtain $313\pm5$ and $695^{+47}_{-45}\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$ in MACS1206. The ICL is blueshifted relative to the BCG by $75\pm22$ and $148\pm38\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$, respectively, and is ~0.7 dex more metal-poor, at a combined statistical significance of ~$2σ$. Defining the ICL as the light fainter than $μ_{B}=25\ \mathrm{mag\ arcsec^{-2}}$ assigns two-thirds to three-quarters of the kinematically defined ICL to the BCG, while a double Sersic model fits the total profiles well but leaves the division between the two components poorly constrained given the depth and resolution of the current MUSE data. Our kinematic decomposition provides a direct, physically motivated reference for photometric definitions of the ICL.

title: The assembly of dusty galaxies at $z \geq 4$: grain growth and the evolutionary origin of the dust-to-stellar-mass scatter
abstract: Understanding dust evolution is essential for interpreting the properties of galaxies across cosmic time. Nearby galaxies have revealed a detailed picture of dust enrichment, but whether the same picture applies in the early Universe remains unclear. Here we explore the origin of interstellar dust in simulated galaxies at $z \sim 5$. Starting from the dust-to-stellar mass relation, we select five simulated star-forming galaxies with $SFR> 1 M_\odot yr^{-1}$ and $ log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 8$. We focus on three low-mass systems with comparable stellar masses ($log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 8.7$) but significantly different dust masses ($log(M_{\rm dust}/M_\odot) \sim 5.1-6.2$), to investigate the origin of the scatter in the relation. Our analysis combines outputs from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulation dustyGadget, a semi-analytical model for stellar dust production, and radiative-transfer post-processing with SKIRT. We confirm that stellar dust production alone reproduces only the low-dust branch of the relation. Grain growth is required to recover both its S-shape and the observed scatter, as established for nearby galaxies. The transition to efficient grain growth occurs at lower metallicity than locally, consistent with the denser interstellar medium of high-redshift systems. Differences in dust content reflect different stages of galaxy assembly. Progressively longer star formation histories lead to greater chemical enrichment and denser ISM, promoting increasingly efficient grain growth. We therefore identify the assembly stage as the key regulator of dust growth at high redshift. Mock observations show that JWST multi-band imaging can reveal the structural diversity of galaxies within the scatter, although the reconstruction of clumpy morphologies may remain incomplete. Their dust continuum emission remains below the sensitivity of current ALMA continuum surveys.

title: Learning Galaxy Kinematics from Spatially Unresolved Spectra
abstract: Galaxy kinematics encode information about the assembly histories of galaxies and the black holes at their centers, motivating the measurement of kinematic parameters for large galaxy populations. In particular, such parameters have been shown to help identify galaxies that host supermassive black hole binaries, a major outstanding question in multi-messenger astrophysics. Yet, inferring kinematic properties from spatially unresolved observations, where distant galaxies appear as point sources, remains a challenge. Spectroscopy can address this challenge because Doppler effects encode internal motions into spectral line profiles. Exploiting this encoding requires knowing how spatial structures map onto the line profiles but this cannot be derived from first principles for complex systems such as galaxies. We present a neural network trained on spatially resolved spectra that infers kinematic properties from spatially integrated spectra, offering two advantages over classical approaches: it learns the kinematic encoding directly from data without requiring spatial resolution and remains effective even when spectral resolution only marginally resolves the lines. This enables recovering the kinematic properties for millions of unresolved galaxies in existing and future surveys.

title: How to feed your dragon: the role of turbulence in AGN activity
abstract: Active galactic nuclei (AGN) are thought to be important drivers of galaxy evolution. However, the way AGN jets couple their energy to the interstellar medium (ISM) remains poorly understood. Recent observations have revealed $\sim$kpc-scale jets in galaxies of different morphological types. Here, we use idealized turbulent box simulations with accreting black holes to investigate how jet-ISM interactions and feedback shape the evolution of jets. We show that a turbulent ISM is a key ingredient in both jet launching and jet propagation. Without turbulence, jet feedback initially shuts off the cold gas supply to the black hole and the system enters a steady state with jet power $\leq 10^{39}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ for a $10^{6}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ black hole. In a turbulent medium, jets fill voids with hot diffuse material which the turbulence then carries away, replenishing the black hole's fuel supply. However, above a critical jet efficiency factor, the jet begins to significantly deplete its fuel supply and enters a self-limiting accretion regime. This critical factor depends on the ISM Mach number, with lower turbulence yielding a lower threshold. Moreover, while the jet power depends on the ambient gas density in the vicinity of the black hole, we find that, at fixed turbulent structure, the morphology and extent of jet propagation are largely insensitive to the average background density; turbulence in the ISM dominates over mean density in setting how far jets propagate, although denser media experience higher total energy injection and stronger heating.

title: Bridging Scales: Multi-Zone GRMHD-Informed Anisotropic AGN Feedback in Galaxies
abstract: We present a galaxy-scale black hole (BH) accretion and feedback model incorporating results from multi-zone general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations spanning the event horizon to the Bondi radius. The model replaces a fixed suppression of the Bondi rate with a nuclear-environment-dependent factor, $κ^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$, set by the local ratio of Bondi to gravitational radius, and distributes outflow mass, kinetic energy, and thermal energy according to the angular structure measured in the large-dynamic-range GRMHD calculations. We apply it to idealized isolated simulations of an M87*-like massive elliptical and a Milky Way/Sgr A*-like galaxy, spanning over three orders of magnitude in BH mass without tuning accretion or feedback efficiencies to match observables. In the M87*-like system, the GRMHD-informed angle-dependent feedback model suppresses late-time stellar mass growth more effectively than the isotropic reference model, despite similar long-term BH accretion rates. Varying the uncertain mass loading of the collimated polar component has a modest impact on BH growth and star formation, indicating that feedback anisotropy matters more than its detailed mass loading. We find that $κ^{\rm hot}_{\rm cho}$ varies with nuclear environment and time, yielding BH growth histories markedly different from fixed-suppression models. For Sgr A*, this variable factor yields an accretion rate more consistent with Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) constraints than a fixed, suppressed Bondi model. These results show that nuclear-environment-dependent accretion and feedback angular structure affect BH-galaxy evolution, requiring subgrid models to include more than a universal Bondi suppression factor and a scalar feedback efficiency.

title: When precise inference is wrong: Diagnosing model misspecification with applications to cosmic dawn and reionisation
abstract: As observations of the cosmic dawn (CD) and epoch of reionisation (EoR) rapidly improve in precision, the approximate forward models used to interpret them might struggle to keep pace. Bayesian inference with a misspecified model, one that cannot represent the processes generating the observations, can yield tightly constrained, yet misleading and biased astrophysics, with different parts of the observations favouring incompatible parameter values. Model misspecification can evade a $χ^2$ goodness-of-fit test, and Bayesian model selection requires a better model, which is not always available. We therefore apply the suspiciousness, a statistic developed to quantify tensions between datasets, to CD/EoR inference as a model criticism tool that tests whether these parts can be explained by the same parameters. We first apply it to HERA 21-cm power spectrum (PS) upper limits, which are too weak to reveal misspecification, as expected, and to HST and JWST UV luminosity functions (LFs). Under our galaxy model, the UV LFs at $z\leq10$ and $z>10$ are in tension at $5.0σ$ in the Gaussian limit, a failure visible in the fits, although doubling the uncertainties of the $z>10$ observations reduces it to $2.1σ$. Finally, we analyse a mock SKA-Low AA$^\ast$ 1080 h 21-cm PS with the model that generated it and with a simpler, misspecified model. We find that the misspecified model silently fails: it fits the PS well, passing visual inspection and, for most noise realisations, a $χ^2$ test, yet its inferred astrophysics is wrong. The Bayesian evidence disfavours it, but only relative to the true model, which is unavailable for real observations. The suspiciousness finds no tension for the well-specified model, but a $\sim3.4σ$ tension for the misspecified one, strongly ruling it out without requiring a more adequate candidate model.

title: SEAMLESS Survey: A Closer Look at Seven Local Volume Dwarf Galaxies in Diverse Environments
abstract: We present Hubble Space Telescope (HST) imaging of six Local Volume dwarf galaxies identified by the SEAMLESS survey - Cetus B, Hydrus A, Ursa Major C, Hydra B, Grapes, and M83-dw14 - along with Centaurus C (Cen C), discovered serendipitously in the M83-dw14 field. We report the discovery of M83-dw14 and Cen C for the first time. Our HST imaging resolves each system into individual stars, enabling measurements of tip of the red giant branch (TRGB) distances (3.6-6.5 Mpc), structural parameters, and star formation histories (SFHs). We complement these data with new HI observations from the Very Large Array for Ursa Major C, Hydra B, and M83-dw14 (also covering Cen C), and from the Green Bank Telescope for Grapes, together with existing HI limits for Cetus B and Hydrus A. With accurate TRGB distances, we place each target in its environmental context, ranging from a confirmed satellite (M83-dw14) to isolated systems (Hydrus A, Hydra B, Grapes, Cen C). Cen C ($M_V=-7.96$) is among the faintest isolated dwarfs known. It matches the size and luminosity of Leo T, the lowest mass gas-rich galaxy currently known, yet unlike Leo T it shows neither detected HI ($\log(M_{\rm HI}/M_{\odot})<5.3$) nor recent star formation. Ursa Major C shows strongly asymmetric, spatially offset HI, suggesting that feedback may efficiently displace gas in such low-mass systems. Overall, our sample exhibits a broad range of SFHs and quenching states that does not track simply with present-day environment. This diversity is consistent with recent evidence that similarly varied SFHs occur even among isolated low-mass dwarfs, pointing to the important roles of inhomogeneous reionization, stochastic mass assembly, and internal feedback alongside environmental effects.

title: Chaos and loss: reevaluating the loss-cone formalism in the context of chaotic diving orbits in flattened potentials
abstract: The region close to a massive black hole is one of the few truly spherical geometries in galactic dynamics. Stellar structures, which dominate from pc to kpc scales, are generally at least flattened (axisymmetric) if not more irregular and time evolving. Here we show that orbits that pass between these diverse geometries are commonly chaotic, especially those which dive - visiting their minimum possible periapse. We show that these chaotic diving orbits are common across a wide range of potentials, and can lead to large variation in angular momentum orbit to orbit. We characterise the transition from regular to chaotic orbits with a notional critical angular momentum, $j_d$. We then model the flux of orbits into the loss cone including the effects of these diving orbits combined with evolution through two-body scattering. Systems which cross into the chaotic region are quickly advected away, and thus there is a large net flux across the boundary. We formulate the problem as a probability density, rather than a number density, allowing us to find a true equilibrium state. We find that the rate of disruptions when including diving orbits is boosted by a multiplicative factor of $1+\ln(j_d/j_t)$, where $j_t$ is the angular momentum corresponding to a disruption. This boost can increase disruption rates by an order of magnitude compared to the classical loss cone formalism.

title: The $δ$ Scuti instability strip and period-luminosity relation as seen by TESS and Gaia DR3
abstract: We present an asteroseismic survey of 1,526,218 A- and F-type stars in and around the $δ$ Scuti instability strip using TESS 10-minute cadence data, which resolve the full $δ$ Scuti pulsation spectra across nearly the entire sky. We derive homogeneous stellar parameters from Gaia DR3 parallaxes and archival photometry, with temperatures that agree with interferometry to within ~300 K. A Positive--Unlabelled classifier identifies 156,706 $δ$ Scuti pulsators, which on average rotate significantly faster than non-variable A-type stars. Within the instability strip in the $T_{eff}$--$\log L$ plane, the pulsator fraction peaks at 30% over the full sample and rises to 80% in the brightest magnitude bins. Detection sensitivity therefore accounts for much, but not all, of the apparent impurity of the strip. Our period--luminosity relation agrees with previous determinations, and we recast it as a scale-invariant period--density relation that connects directly to the pulsation constant. We find that the secondary ridge in these relations is probably a combination of several overtone modes. The $δ$ Scuti stars closest to the fundamental ridge have systematically lower rotational velocities and occupy a distinct region of the instability strip. Finally, a cross-match with a Gaia catalog of open clusters reveals a correlation between the mean pulsation frequency of $δ$ Scuti stars and cluster age, suggesting a new ensemble asteroseismic age indicator for young stellar populations.

title: PRISMS GHZ8: Evidence for a Young Burst and Potential Merger Activity at z=10.23
abstract: UV-bright galaxies in the early Universe provide important constraints on the rapid build-up of stellar mass and the sources responsible for cosmic reionization. However, the physical processes that drive their high UV luminosities remain unclear. Here we report JWST/MIRI LRS spectroscopy of GHZ8, a UV-bright galaxy at z=10.23 with a magnification $μ=1.23$. The spectrum shows a $\sim 5σ$ detection for the $\rm Hβ$-[OIII] complex and $\sim 4σ$ for $\rm Hα$ line, with fluxes of $3.2\pm0.9\times10^{-18}$ and $\rm 1.7\pm0.4\times10^{-18}\,erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$, respectively. Based on JWST/NIRCam imaging, we find that GHZ8 consists of two components separated only by 0.16" ($\approx600$ pc): a bright, extended main component and a faint, compact southeastern clump, hereafter referred to as GHZ8-main and GHZ8-SE. Through morphological decomposition, we find demagnified $M_{UV}=-19.91\pm0.10$ and $-18.03\pm0.15$ mag for GHZ8-main and GHZ8-SE, with blue UV slopes of $β_{UV}=-2.53\pm0.22$ and $-3.45\pm0.49$, respectively, indicating that both components host young stellar populations. In particular, the extremely blue UV continuum of GHZ8-SE requires an extremely young, ISM-poor stellar population with a high ionizing photon escape fraction, $f_{esc}= 0.6-1.0$. Combining the UV and $\rm Hα$ luminosities with the results from the spectro-photometric SED fitting, we constrain the star-formation activity of GHZ8-main, and find either a recent, short-lived burst of star formation that is now in its final phases, or continuous star formation over a relatively short period ($<50\,{\rm Myr}$). GHZ8 therefore provides observational evidence for bursty star formation in a UV-bright galaxy. Globally, GHZ8 may be undergoing a merger-induced starburst, although deeper imaging or spatially resolved kinematic information is required for a more definitive interpretation.
